For example: “₹50 off for you and ₹50 off for your friend.” Or a club gets a discount for using your product on its trips. A short note lists what you changed in the AI drafts and why.

reflection.prompt: Who has already helped you this year, even in a small way? How could you thank them, or give something back, before you ask for anything new?
reflection.hint: Strong networks are built on giving as well as asking. A short update on what their help led to is a good thank-you.

workbook.hook: The person who can help you most is probably one introduction away.
idea: You have a bigger network than you think: people you know, your campus, your city, and people online. Map them, with what you can ask and what you can offer.
The best way to meet someone new is a double opt-in introduction: the connector asks them first. Make it easy with a short message the connector can forward as it is.
On LinkedIn, send a few specific notes. Grow through referrals and partnerships where each side gains something.
why: Introductions get replies that cold messages don’t
Mentors and partners can save you months of mistakes
Referred customers can cost less, and trust you sooner
workbook.simple: When a family new to a city needs a good doctor, they don’t search the whole internet. They ask a neighbour, who asks her cousin. The cousin checks that the doctor takes new patients, then passes on the number.

myth.wrong: Networking means collecting as many contacts as possible.
myth.right: A few people you help and keep in touch with are worth more than hundreds of strangers. Specific asks and small offers build the relationship.

example.title: Notebooks and a 15-minute call
example.body: Imagine Wasim in Bareilly, who sells notebooks made from recycled paper. He wants advice on selling to schools. A teacher at his college knows Nandini, who supplies stationery to schools. Wasim writes a note the teacher can forward: “I make recycled-paper notebooks in Bareilly and have sold 300 to students. I’d like 15 minutes to ask how you won your first school order.” The teacher checks with Nandini first, and she agrees. After the call, Wasim thanks the teacher and tells him what he learned.

terms.meaning: Someone who knows both people and makes the introduction.
The connector asks the other person first, and introduces you only if they agree.
A short note the connector can forward without changing a word.
A programme that gives early founders mentors, space and sometimes small grants.
A happy customer brings a friend, often with a reward for both.
An agreement with another group that serves the same customers, where each side gains.

try_it.title: Make an ask forwardable
try_it.prompt: Rewrite this message so a teacher can forward it, word for word, to the owner of a sports academy. The message: “Hi, can you connect me to someone who knows about coaching?” About me: I run a weekend football session for children in an Indian city. I want 15 minutes of advice on how to set fees. Keep it under 80 words. Use [brackets] for any numbers I need to fill in.
try_it.look_for: Does it say who you are, why this person, the exact ask and how much time it needs?
try_it.check: Fill in only real numbers. Then read it as the academy owner: could you say yes in one reply? Cut any flattery and anything you can’t back up.

try_it.title: Design a referral offer
try_it.prompt: I run a small custom T-shirt printing business in an Indian city. Suggest 3 referral offers where both the customer and their friend get something. For each, say what one new customer would cost me.
try_it.look_for: Does each offer reward both people? Is the cost of one new customer clear?
try_it.check: Work out each cost yourself: add the two rewards. Compare it with what one customer costs through your other channel. Keep the cheapest offer that still feels generous.

workbook.tip: After any introduction, tell the connector what happened within a week. People who hear back are glad to introduce you again.
workbook.mistake: Asking a stranger for something vague, like “guidance” or “a quick chat”. Say what you want to learn, and what you can offer.

checks.scenario: Meenal in Tirupati wants to start a home-made jam brand. She is choosing whom to contact first from her network map.
checks.question: Who is most likely to reply and help?
options: A senior who ran a campus snack stall last year
The owner of a national jam brand she admires
A food blogger in Tirupati with two lakh followers
Her cousin, who works in a bank and loves her jam
checks.hint: Think about how many messages each person gets, and how recent and useful their lessons would be.
checks.why: A senior one step ahead gets few requests, and her lessons are recent, so she is likely to reply with useful advice. A national founder and a big blogger get many messages. Her cousin will reply, but has never sold anything.

checks.scenario: Kartik sells bottled cold coffee in Puducherry. He wants his customers to bring their friends.
checks.question: When should he ask a customer to refer a friend?
options: In his first message, before they have tried it
Once a month, in a broadcast to every contact
Right after a delivery the customer was happy with
Only after they have bought ten bottles from him
checks.hint: Think about the customer’s mood at each moment, and what they could tell a friend.
checks.why: Ask right after a good moment, such as a happy delivery: the customer has something real to share. Before trying it, they have nothing to tell. A broadcast isn’t a personal ask at a good moment. Waiting for ten bottles misses most happy customers.

checks.scenario: Ayaan wants advice from an alumna. She wrote a public LinkedIn post about how her small online business found its first 100 customers.
checks.question: Which invitation note is best?
options: Your post on your first 100 customers was great. Could we do a one-hour call on your whole journey?
Your post on your first 100 customers helped me. Could I ask one question about it?
Hi, I’m building a startup in Lucknow and saw your post. Could you guide me?
You are an inspiration to all of us students. Could you share some general tips with me?
checks.hint: Read each note as the alumna. Could she tell why he chose her, and answer in one reply?
checks.why: It shows why he chose her and asks for something she can answer in one reply. A one-hour call on her whole journey is too big an ask from a stranger. “Guide me” and “general tips” don’t say what he wants to learn.

quiz.title: Asking for an introduction
quiz.scenario: Rhea in Bhopal runs baking classes with 30 paying students. She wants advice on running classes online. Her E-cell mentor knows Kavita Menon, who runs a large online cooking channel.
quiz.question: Which message to her mentor is best for him to forward?
options: “Could you ask Kavita if she’d take a 15-minute call? I teach baking in Bhopal to 30 paying students and want to ask how she moved online.”
“Could you connect me with someone who knows about online classes? Anyone at all would really help me, and I’m flexible about when we talk.”
“Please send Kavita my number and my full business plan. I would love her to invest in my classes, or to partner with me on her channel.”
“Hi! I’m Rhea, a huge fan of Kavita’s channel. Could you add the three of us to a WhatsApp group so that we can all chat about baking sometime?”
quiz.explanation: It can be forwarded as it is: who Rhea is, why Kavita, one specific question and how much time it needs. Kavita can say yes or no in one reply.
quiz.why_wrong: “Someone who knows about online classes” is too vague for the mentor to act on. Sending her number and plan and asking for investment is a big ask of a stranger, with no agreed time. A group chat connects them before Kavita has agreed, and “chat sometime” has no clear ask.
quiz.learning_outcome: Write introduction requests that are specific and forwardable.

quiz.title: An introduction from the incubator
quiz.scenario: Your college incubator’s manager offers to introduce you to an alumnus who runs a D2C skincare brand. You want to ask him how he found his first stockists.
quiz.question: What should you ask the manager to do, if you want a double opt-in introduction?
options: Ask the alumnus first, and connect you both only if he agrees to talk
Give you the alumnus’s phone number, so that you can call him yourself
Add the two of you to a WhatsApp group with a short introduction
Email the alumnus with you in copy, attaching your full pitch deck
quiz.explanation: In a double opt-in introduction, the connector checks with the other person before connecting you. The alumnus agrees first, so he is ready to help when you write, and the manager’s trust with him is protected.
quiz.why_wrong: Sharing his number without asking puts him on the spot and uses up the manager’s goodwill. A WhatsApp group and an email in copy both connect you before he has agreed, and a full pitch deck turns a small question into a large ask.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask connectors for double opt-in introductions.

quiz.title: Two hundred invitations a day
quiz.scenario: Sanjay wants advice from founders who studied at his college. A friend suggests a browser tool that sends 200 LinkedIn invitations a day, each with the same message.
quiz.question: What is the better approach?
options: Use the tool, since sending more invitations means more founders will reply
Send all 200 invitations by hand without notes, so that no tool is involved
Use AI to change the name in each note, then send all 200 with the tool
Choose a few founders and write each one a short note about their own work
quiz.explanation: A few specific notes, each mentioning something the founder shared publicly, get more replies than a mass of identical ones. LinkedIn’s Help Centre also says automation tools are not allowed and that many ignored invitations can restrict an account.
quiz.why_wrong: The tool breaks LinkedIn’s rules, and identical messages get ignored, which can restrict his account. Sending 200 by hand without notes is still a mass of invitations to people with no reason to accept. Changing only the name is still a mass message, sent by a tool that isn’t allowed.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reach out to a few people with specific notes, never in bulk.

quiz.title: Referral or Instagram
quiz.scenario: Ishaan in Shillong sells a monthly snack box. Last month, ₹1,800 of Instagram posts brought him 12 new customers. Now he offers referrals: ₹40 off for the customer and ₹40 off for the friend they bring.
quiz.question: What does one new customer cost through each channel?
options: Referral ₹40 and Instagram ₹150
Referral ₹80 and Instagram ₹1,800
Referral ₹80 and Instagram ₹150
Referral ₹40 and Instagram ₹1,800
quiz.explanation: Each referral gives ₹40 to the customer and ₹40 to the friend, so one new customer costs ₹80. Instagram cost ₹1,800 ÷ 12 = ₹150 a customer. Referrals are cheaper, and the friends arrive already trusting the product.
quiz.why_wrong: ₹40 counts only the friend’s discount and forgets the ₹40 given to the customer who referred them. ₹1,800 is the whole month’s Instagram spend, not the cost of one customer: divide it by the 12 customers it brought.
quiz.learning_outcome: Work out the cost of one new customer for each channel.

modules.title: Price and manage money
modules.summary: Set a price from what customers value, check you earn on every sale, include payment fees, plan cash week by week, and know how first funding works.
modules.outcome: Set a price and show in a rupee table that each customer earns back more than they cost to win, with a one-month cash-flow plan.

learn.title: Price from value, not just from cost
learn.body:
Many first founders add a markup to their cost and call it the price. This is called cost-plus pricing. It ignores what the product is worth to the customer.

Think of two limits. The floor is your cost for each unit: below it, you lose money on every sale. The ceiling is what the customer would pay for the next best option. Your price sits between them, set by the value of the problem you solve.

Worked example: Divya in Jaipur runs mock interviews for students before placement season. Each one-hour session costs her about ₹150 in calls, materials and a reviewer’s time. A coaching institute charges ₹2,000 a session. Free YouTube videos give no personal feedback. In her interviews, three students had paid ₹1,500 for a CV review. She chose ₹499 a session, or ₹1,299 for three.

Common mistake: pricing very low “because students can’t pay”, without asking them.

learn.title: Unit economics: do you earn on each sale?
learn.body:
Unit economics means the money in and out for one unit: one sale or one customer.

Contribution margin is the price minus the costs that come with each unit, such as ingredients, packaging, delivery and payment fees. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is your marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it brought.

Worked example: a campus tiffin service.
Price per meal: ₹120.
Ingredients ₹55 + packaging ₹8 + delivery ₹15 = ₹78.
Contribution per meal: ₹120 − ₹78 = ₹42.
It spent ₹1,000 on posters and samples and won 20 customers, so CAC = ₹1,000 ÷ 20 = ₹50.
If a customer orders 8 meals a month, they bring 8 × ₹42 = ₹336. That is well above ₹50.
If they order only once, ₹42 is less than ₹50: a loss.

So repeat orders matter as much as price. AI can set up this table in Google Sheets, but check its sums by hand.

learn.title: Count payment fees, and date them
learn.body:
Payment fees come out of every sale, so they belong in your unit economics. They change, so check the provider’s own page and write the date in your sheet.

UPI (checked 21 November 2026): NPCI’s FAQ of 15 September 2026 sets a fee of 0.4%, capped at ₹300, on UPI payments to merchants above ₹2,000. Payments up to ₹2,000, and payments between people, stay free. Small sellers receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month by UPI QR pay nothing. Sellers can’t pass the fee on to customers. NPCI has said the fee will start after Diwali, on a date it will notify. No date has been set yet, so check npci.org.in.
Worked example: Jaspreet’s ₹1,200 phone stands are under ₹2,000, so UPI adds no fee.

Payment gateways handle cards, wallets and payment links. Razorpay’s pricing page (October 2026) lists 2% of each payment plus 18% GST on that fee for its standard plan.
Worked example: on a ₹1,000 order, fee ₹20 + GST ₹3.60 = ₹23.60. You receive ₹976.40.

learn.title: Plan cash week by week
learn.body:
Profit and cash are different. You can make a profit on paper and still run out of cash, because you pay for stock before customers pay you. Many young businesses fail this way.

A cash-flow plan lists money in and money out, week by week, and the cash left at the end of each week.

Worked example: Sneha in Bhubaneswar starts a candle business with ₹10,000 of savings.
Week 1: buys wax and jars for ₹7,000, sells ₹1,500. Cash left: ₹4,500.
Week 2: marketing ₹1,000, sells ₹2,500. Cash left: ₹6,000.
Week 3: more stock ₹4,000, sells ₹3,000. Cash left: ₹5,000.
Week 4: sells ₹3,500. Cash left: ₹8,500.
Her lowest point is week 1, not the end of the month.

Runway is how many months your cash lasts if you keep losing money at today’s rate. Cash ÷ monthly loss = runway in months. Example: ₹6,000 left and losing ₹2,000 a month gives 3 months of runway.

learn.title: How first funding works
learn.body:
Most student businesses start with their own money, in this rough order.
1. Bootstrapping: your savings and your sales. Pre-orders count too.
2. Friends and family. Write down whether the money is a gift, a loan with a repayment date, or a share of the business.
3. Competitions, college grants and incubator programmes. Ask your E-cell or incubator. Schemes open and close, so check that one is open on its official page.
4. Bank loans. For example, banks lend to small businesses under the PM MUDRA Yojana. Check the current limits on its official site.
5. Angel investors and venture capital funds. They buy shares and expect fast growth. They are rare at the idea stage, and they look for evidence such as paying customers.

Worked example: an investor offers ₹5 lakh for 10% of your business. That values the business at ₹5 lakh ÷ 10% = ₹50 lakh, including the investor’s ₹5 lakh.

Common mistake: chasing investors before you have customers.

tasks.title: Check a business’s unit economics
tasks.prompt:
Sneha sells scented candles through Instagram messages for ₹349 each, paid by UPI. Each candle costs her ₹120 in wax, jar and fragrance, ₹25 in packaging, and about ₹60 for delivery within the city. Last month she spent ₹2,000 on a boosted post and free samples and won 16 new customers. On average, a customer buys 1.5 candles in three months.
In Google Sheets (free) or on paper, work out:
1. The contribution per candle.
2. Her CAC.
3. The contribution from one customer over three months.
Then decide whether she earns back what each customer costs, and suggest two changes that would improve the numbers.
tasks.hint: Total the costs that come with each candle first. Do UPI fees apply to a ₹349 payment? Check the dated card. Then compare one customer’s contribution with what it cost to win them.
tasks.after: Costs per candle: ₹120 + ₹25 + ₹60 = ₹205. Contribution: ₹349 − ₹205 = ₹144. A ₹349 UPI payment is under ₹2,000, so there is no UPI fee. CAC: ₹2,000 ÷ 16 = ₹125. One customer over three months: 1.5 × ₹144 = ₹216. So yes, she earns back what each customer costs, with ₹91 to spare. But a customer who buys only once brings ₹144 against ₹125, which is thin. Good changes: more repeat orders, such as a refill offer or a set of two. Lower delivery cost, by grouping deliveries by area or using a pickup point. Or cheaper customers, through referrals.

tasks.title: Price your offer and plan one month’s cash
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea:
1. Write your price floor (cost per unit), your ceiling (the next best option’s price) and your price, with one line of reason.
2. In Google Sheets (free), make a four-week cash-flow plan: starting cash, money in (sales, pre-orders, family money), money out (stock, marketing, delivery, fees, tools) and cash left each week.
3. Mark your lowest week, and name one source of first money that suits your stage, with a reason.
Ask a free AI chatbot which costs you might have missed, then check each suggestion against your real plan.
tasks.hint: Be honest about when money arrives. A pre-order paid today is cash this week; a promise to pay next month is not. Write the date next to every fee you looked up.
tasks.after: A good answer gives a floor from real costs per unit, and a ceiling from the next best option’s price. The price sits between them, with a reason from interviews. The Sheet has starting cash, money in and money out for each week. It shows the cash left at the end of each week. Money counts only in the week it arrives. The lowest week is marked; it is often the week stock is bought. The source of first money fits the stage. Examples: savings and pre-orders, family money written down as a gift or a loan, or a college competition open now. Every fee has the date it was checked.

reflection.prompt: Would you rather start with your own small savings, family money, or an investor’s money? What would each one cost you, apart from rupees?
reflection.hint: Think about control, pressure and relationships. Family money can strain a relationship; investor money means sharing ownership and decisions.

workbook.hook: You can sell a lot and still run out of money. Learn the numbers that stop that.
idea: Set your price between a floor and a ceiling. The floor is what each unit costs you. The ceiling is what the customer pays for the next best option. Where your price sits depends on the value of the problem you solve.
Check your unit economics. Contribution is the price minus the costs that come with each unit. Compare it with your CAC: what it costs to win a customer.
Profit and cash are different. Plan cash week by week, because you often pay for stock before customers pay you.
why: You avoid losing money on every sale without noticing
You see whether repeat orders or price matter more
You spot your lowest cash week before it arrives
workbook.simple: An auto driver knows his fuel cost for a trip to the station, and what the bus fare is. He quotes a fare between the two. He also keeps enough cash to fill the tank each morning, before the day’s fares come in.

myth.wrong: If I’m making a profit, I can’t run out of money.
myth.right: Profit is on paper. Cash is what you have this week. You can be profitable and still have no cash to buy stock.

example.title: Fruit bowls, before and after the sums
example.body: Tejas in Raipur sells cut-fruit bowls to office workers for ₹90. Before: “Lots of people buy my bowls, so I must be doing well.” After he works it out: Cost per bowl: ₹40 fruit + ₹6 box + ₹14 delivery = ₹60. Contribution: ₹90 − ₹60 = ₹30 a bowl. CAC: ₹1,200 on flyers and samples ÷ 24 customers = ₹50. A customer who buys 10 bowls a month brings ₹300, far above ₹50. One who buys once brings ₹30, less than ₹50. So he works hardest at bringing customers back.

terms.meaning: Your cost for each unit. Below it, every sale loses money.
What the customer would pay for the next best option.
Price minus the costs that come with each unit sold.
Marketing spend divided by the new customers it brought.
Money in and money out, week by week, with the cash left each week.
How many months your cash lasts at today’s rate of loss: cash ÷ monthly loss.

try_it.title: Build a unit-economics table
try_it.prompt: Make a simple table I can paste into Google Sheets for a business selling hand-made notebooks at ₹180 each. Costs per notebook: paper ₹50, binding ₹20, packaging ₹10, delivery ₹30. Last month, ₹1,500 of marketing brought 20 new customers. Each customer buys 2 notebooks on average. Ignore payment fees. Show the contribution per notebook, the CAC and the contribution per customer, with the formulas.
try_it.look_for: Does it use only the costs that come with each notebook, and divide the marketing spend by new customers?
try_it.check: Do the sums by hand. ₹180 − ₹110 = ₹70 per notebook. ₹1,500 ÷ 20 = ₹75 CAC. 2 × ₹70 = ₹140 per customer, more than ₹75. If the AI’s numbers differ, find its mistake before you use its table.

try_it.title: Find the costs you forgot
try_it.prompt: I’m planning a four-week cash flow for a small business selling hand-painted diyas before Diwali in India. List the costs a first-time seller often forgets, and say which ones are paid before the sales come in.
try_it.look_for: Does it mention costs such as packaging, delivery, breakage, samples and payment fees?
try_it.check: Keep only the costs that fit your real plan. For any fee it names, check the provider’s own page and write today’s date next to it, because fees change.

workbook.tip: Write the date next to every fee and price you look up. When something changes, you’ll know which numbers to check again.
workbook.mistake: Pricing very low “because students can’t pay”, without asking what they already pay for the next best option.

checks.scenario: Vani in Hubballi teaches one-hour guitar lessons online. Each lesson costs her about ₹80 in internet and materials. A music school nearby charges ₹600 a lesson.
checks.question: What is her price floor?
options: ₹600, what the music school charges
₹80, what each lesson costs her
₹340, halfway between cost and the school
₹0, because online lessons need no stock
checks.hint: Below which price would she lose money on every lesson?
checks.why: The floor is her cost for each unit: about ₹80. The school’s ₹600 is her ceiling. Halfway is a possible price, not a floor, and online lessons still have costs.

checks.scenario: Selvi runs a tailoring business in Vellore. She buys fabric when she takes an order, and customers pay when they collect their clothes two weeks later. Her May accounts show a profit, but on 10 June she can’t afford new fabric.
checks.question: What is the most likely reason?
options: Her prices are too high, so customers stopped ordering
Her bank is holding back her UPI money for a month
She counted wrongly, since a profit means cash in hand
She pays for fabric about two weeks before she is paid
checks.hint: Think about the difference between making a profit and having cash.
checks.why: Money goes out for fabric two weeks before customers pay. So cash can run short even when the business makes a profit. Nothing in the case points to falling orders or a bank delay, and profit isn’t the same as cash.

checks.scenario: Om has ₹9,000 in the bank. His small business is losing ₹3,000 a month.
checks.question: How many months of runway does he have?
options: 3 months
6 months
2 months
1 month
checks.hint: Runway is cash divided by monthly loss.
checks.why: ₹9,000 ÷ ₹3,000 = 3 months. Six months comes from subtracting instead of dividing (₹9,000 − ₹3,000). Two months takes off this month’s loss first (₹6,000 ÷ ₹3,000). One month divides the loss by itself.

quiz.title: Pricing mock discussions
quiz.scenario: Kunal in Chandigarh runs one-hour mock group discussions for MBA entrance students. Each session costs him about ₹180 to run. A coaching centre charges ₹1,200 a session. In his interviews, four students had paid seniors ₹600 to ₹800 for one-off sessions.
quiz.question: Which price is best supported by these facts?
options: ₹220: his ₹180 cost plus a 20% markup
₹99: students can’t afford to pay more
₹699: near what students already pay
₹1,500: a high price looks premium
quiz.explanation: His floor is the ₹180 cost and his ceiling is the coaching centre’s ₹1,200. ₹699 sits between them, close to what students already pay seniors, so it matches the value they place on a session. He should still test it with real buyers.
quiz.why_wrong: Cost plus 20% ignores what the session is worth to the buyer and leaves most of that value unearned. ₹99 is a guess about what students can pay, and his interviews show they already pay far more. ₹1,500 is above the next best option, so buyers would choose the coaching centre.
quiz.learning_outcome: Price between cost and the next best option, guided by what customers value.

quiz.title: Breakfast boxes
quiz.scenario: Megha sells breakfast boxes to hostel students for ₹250 each. Each box costs her ₹90 in food, ₹20 in packaging and ₹30 in delivery. She spent ₹3,000 on posters and samples and won 20 customers. On average, a customer buys 2 boxes. Ignore payment fees here.
quiz.question: Does she earn back what each customer cost her to win?
options: Yes: each customer brings ₹220 of contribution against a CAC of ₹150
No: each box brings ₹110 of contribution, which is less than the ₹150 CAC
Yes: each customer brings ₹500 of sales against a CAC of only ₹150
No: her CAC is ₹3,000, more than any one customer will ever bring
quiz.explanation: Contribution per box is ₹250 − ₹140 = ₹110. A customer buys 2 boxes, so brings ₹220. CAC is ₹3,000 ÷ 20 = ₹150. ₹220 is more than ₹150, so each customer earns back their cost, with ₹70 to spare.
quiz.why_wrong: Comparing one box’s ₹110 with the CAC forgets the second order. ₹500 is sales, not contribution: it ignores the ₹140 of costs in each box. ₹3,000 is the whole marketing spend; CAC divides it by the 20 customers it won.
quiz.learning_outcome: Compare one customer’s total contribution with the cost of winning them.

quiz.title: Last year’s fee
quiz.scenario: Arnav is building his unit-economics table in Google Sheets. For the payment-gateway fee, he copied a percentage from a blog post written last year.
quiz.question: What should he do about the fee?
options: Leave fees out of the table, since they are too small to matter
Keep the blog’s figure, since gateway fees rarely change much
Check the gateway’s own pricing page today, and note the date
Ask an AI chatbot for the current fee, and use the figure it gives
quiz.explanation: Fees change, so the reliable figure is on the provider’s own page, checked now. Writing the date next to it shows when to check again. The fee then goes into the cost of every sale in his table.
quiz.why_wrong: Fees come out of every sale, so leaving them out makes each sale look better than it is. A blog figure from last year may be out of date, because fees do change. An AI chatbot can give an old or invented figure, so its answer still needs checking on the provider’s page.
quiz.learning_outcome: Take fees from the provider’s own page, dated, and include them in costs.

quiz.title: Cash in week two
quiz.scenario:
Nisha starts selling block-printed dupattas with ₹8,000 of savings. Her four-week plan:
Week 1: ₹9,000 out (stock), ₹2,000 in.
Week 2: ₹2,500 out, ₹1,000 in.
Week 3: ₹1,000 out, ₹6,000 in.
Week 4: ₹500 out, ₹7,000 in.
quiz.question: What does her plan show?
options: The month ends at ₹11,000, more than she started with, so it needs no change
Her lowest point is week 1, at ₹1,000, so she is safe if week 1 goes well
She loses money over the month, as ₹13,000 goes out against ₹8,000 saved
Her cash falls below zero in week 2, so she must plan for that week now
quiz.explanation: Week by week: ₹8,000 − ₹9,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹1,000 after week 1, then ₹1,000 − ₹2,500 + ₹1,000 = −₹500 after week 2. She needs ₹500 more by then, or must move a cost later, even though the month ends at ₹11,000.
quiz.why_wrong: The month-end total hides week 2, when she can’t pay her costs. Week 1 is not the lowest point: week 2 goes ₹500 below zero. The ₹13,000 going out should be set against ₹16,000 of sales as well as her savings; over the month she ends ahead.
quiz.learning_outcome: Plan cash week by week: a profitable month can still run out of cash.

modules.title: Build your team
modules.summary: Choose co-founders well, split equity with vesting, agree who decides what, and work fairly with freelancers and interns.
modules.outcome: Write a team plan for your idea: who owns each area, the equity split and vesting you have or would offer a co-founder, and a first brief for a freelancer or intern.

learn.title: Choosing a co-founder
learn.body:
A co-founder is a partner who builds the business with you and owns part of it. Look for three things.
1. Skills that complement yours. One person builds the product, the other sells it.
2. The same commitment: hours each week, and a plan for what happens after placement offers.
3. Shared values about money, risk and honesty.

Test the partnership before you commit. Work together on a small project for two weeks, such as running your MVP test.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya in Chennai want to build a revision app for Class 12 students. Arjun codes; Priya has already sold 40 pre-orders to parents. Before agreeing to be co-founders, they asked each other: “How many hours a week can you give? What if one of us takes a job offer? How will we settle a disagreement?”

Common mistake: choosing your closest friend without having these conversations.

learn.title: Equity and vesting, written down early
learn.body:
Equity is ownership of the business, counted in shares. Common advice, including from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, is to split it nearly equally between founders who commit fully. Then add vesting.

Vesting means you earn your shares over time. A common plan is four years with a one-year cliff. If you leave before the first year ends, you keep none. At one year, a quarter vests. The rest vests month by month.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya split 50:50 with that plan. If Priya leaves after 18 months, she has earned 18 of 48 months: 18 ÷ 48 = 37.5% of her shares. That is 37.5% × 50% = 18.75% of the business. The unearned shares stay with the business for whoever does the work.

Common mistake: a spoken deal with no vesting. Write it down and both sign it now. You can make it formal when you register the business.

learn.title: Roles, decisions and how you work
learn.body:
Most fights between founders are about who decides. Give each area one owner. The owner listens to others, then decides.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya wrote this down.
Arjun owns the product and technology.
Priya owns sales, marketing and money.
They decide together on hiring, fundraising and anything above ₹10,000.
If they disagree on a joint decision, each writes down their reasons, they sleep on it, and then they ask their mentor.

Culture is simply how you work together. Write down three habits, and act on them. For example: “We reply to customers within two hours.” “We write every decision in a shared Google Doc.” “We never post fake reviews.”

AI can help. Paste your rough notes into a free chatbot and ask for a one-page roles document. Then check that it says what you agreed, not what the AI assumed. Common mistake: “we both do everything”.

learn.title: Freelancers and interns, done fairly
learn.body:
You don’t need full-time staff to start. A freelancer is paid for a piece of work. An intern works with you to learn.

For a freelancer, write a brief: the goal, the exact deliverables, the deadline, the budget and examples you like. Pay per deliverable, often half at the start and half on delivery, by UPI. Agree that you receive the original files.

Worked example: Priya’s brief for a designer: “A logo and three Instagram post templates for a Class 12 revision app. Deadline: 10 days. Budget: ₹4,000, half now and half on delivery. Send the Canva or Figma files with the final versions.”

For an intern, write a brief too. Include the work, the hours, what they will learn, who will guide them and the pay, agreed before they start. Common mistake: vague “help with marketing” internships, where the intern learns little and you get little done.

tasks.title: Advise three would-be co-founders
tasks.prompt:
Three friends in Nagpur are starting a delivery service for home-made pickles. Rahul will work full-time after graduating next month and builds the website. Ayesha is in her final year, gives 15 hours a week, and has made all 30 sales so far. Varun had the idea, gives about 5 hours a week, and starts a job in three months. They want to split equity 33:33:33 with nothing written down.
Write them a short note (under 200 words):
1. Who should be a co-founder, and who might be better as an adviser or early helper, with reasons.
2. A suggested split and vesting plan.
3. Three questions they must answer together this week.
tasks.hint: Compare commitment and contribution, not who had the idea. Ask what happens to Varun’s shares when his job starts. Vesting is the tool that answers that fairly.
tasks.after: A strong note says Rahul and Ayesha look like co-founders. Rahul builds the website and will work full-time. Ayesha has made every sale so far. She gives 15 hours a week until she graduates, so they should agree her hours after that before settling the split. Varun had the idea, but gives 5 hours a week and starts a job in three months. He may fit better as an adviser or early helper, perhaps with a small share that also vests. If Ayesha will be full-time too, a fair split might be 45:45:10. Everyone vests over four years with a one-year cliff, written down and signed. Questions for this week: How many hours will each of us give after Varun’s job starts? What happens to shares if someone leaves? Who owns which area, and how do we settle a disagreement?

tasks.title: Write your team plan, a hiring brief and team habits
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea:
1. Write who owns each area of your business (product, sales, money). If you have, or want, a co-founder, write the split and vesting you would propose, in two lines. Working alone? Write the split and vesting you would offer a co-founder.
2. Write a one-page brief for a freelancer or an intern you might need in the next month: the goal, deliverables, deadline, pay and how it is paid, who reviews the work, and (for an intern) what they will learn.
3. Write three habits for how your team works.
Write your points as rough notes first, then ask a free AI chatbot to turn them into a clear brief. Check that it promises nothing you can’t pay for or deliver.
tasks.hint: For the split, use the same test as for the pickle founders: commitment and contribution, with vesting. A good brief lets a stranger start work without asking you a question. Read yours as if you were the freelancer: is anything unclear?
tasks.after: A good answer gives each area one named owner, not “both of us”. The split and vesting fit in two lines. For example: “50:50, vesting over four years with a one-year cliff, then monthly.” The brief lets a stranger start without asking anything. It gives the goal, exact deliverables, deadline and pay. It says how the pay is made, for example half now and half on delivery, by UPI. It names who reviews the work. An intern brief also gives the hours, who guides them and what they will learn. The three habits are specific actions, such as “We reply to customers within two hours.”

reflection.prompt: What are you bad at, or don’t enjoy, that your business still needs? Who could do it, and what would make it fair for them?
reflection.hint: Founders often hire people like themselves. The best early partners are often strong where you are weak.

workbook.hook: A great idea can fall apart over one question: who owns what? Settle it while you’re still friends.
idea: Choose co-founders for complementary skills, the same commitment and shared values. Test working together on something small before you commit.
Split equity, then add vesting, so shares are earned over time. A common plan is four years with a one-year cliff. Write it down now.
Give every area one owner, who decides after listening. Brief freelancers and interns clearly: the goal, the deliverables, the deadline, the pay, and what an intern will learn.
why: Clear owners end daily arguments
Vesting keeps the split fair if someone leaves
A clear brief gets good work the first time
workbook.simple: In a cricket team, the captain sets the field and the keeper calls the catches near the stumps. Big calls, like the batting order, are agreed before the match. So nobody argues mid-over about who decides.

myth.wrong: Best friends make the best co-founders, so we don’t need anything in writing.
myth.right: Friendship helps, but you still need the same commitment, a written split with vesting, and clear owners. Writing it down protects the friendship.

example.title: A CV-review service, twenty months in
example.body: Imagine Tanya and Farhan in Visakhapatnam, starting a CV-review service. They split 50:50, with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff. They write it on one page, and both sign it. Tanya owns sales and money; Farhan owns the service and its quality. Anything above ₹5,000 they decide together. Twenty months in, Farhan takes a full-time job and leaves. He has earned 20 of 48 months: about 42% of his shares, or about 21% of the business. The rest stays with the business for whoever does the work. There is no fight, because they agreed it at the start.

terms.meaning: A partner who builds the business with you and owns part of it.
Ownership of the business, counted in shares.
Earning your shares over time, instead of all at once.
The first period, often one year, before any shares vest at all.
The one person who decides in an area, after listening to others.
A written description of the work: goal, deliverables, deadline and pay.

try_it.title: Turn notes into a roles page
try_it.prompt: Turn these rough notes into a one-page roles document for two founders of a college event-photography business. Founder A edits photos and looks after the equipment. Founder B finds clients and handles money. We decide together on hiring and anything above ₹8,000. If we disagree, we each write our reasons, sleep on it, and ask our mentor. Habits: reply to clients within 3 hours; record every decision in a shared Google Doc. Don’t add anything we haven’t agreed.
try_it.look_for: Does it keep exactly what you agreed, or does it add titles, salaries or rules you never discussed?
try_it.check: Delete anything the AI assumed. Check that each area has one owner, and that “we both do everything” hasn’t crept back in.

try_it.title: Check a vesting sum
try_it.prompt: Two founders split their company 50:50, with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff, vesting monthly after the cliff. If one founder leaves after 24 months, what share of the whole business has she earned? Show the working.
try_it.look_for: Does it use 24 of 48 months, and then apply that to her 50%?
try_it.check: Work it out yourself. 24 ÷ 48 = 50% of her shares. 50% × 50% = 25% of the business. Had she left before 12 months, the answer would be 0%.

workbook.tip: Ask the hard questions in week one. How many hours will each of you give? What happens after a job offer? How will you settle a disagreement?
workbook.mistake: Giving an intern “help with marketing” and nothing more. Without set work, hours, a guide and agreed pay, they learn little and you get little done.

checks.scenario: Dhruv and Mehak in Mumbai are splitting their startup 50:50. Mehak may take a job offer in six months, but neither knows yet.
checks.question: What should they add to their written split?
options: Four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, for both of them
A 60:40 split now, with more for whoever is likelier to stay
Nothing yet: they will write it all down when they register
A bigger share now for whichever of them had the idea first
checks.hint: For each option, picture Mehak leaving in six months. What happens to her shares?
checks.why: With vesting, shares are earned over time, so someone who leaves early keeps only what they have earned. A different split now doesn’t change what happens when someone leaves. Waiting to register leaves a spoken deal. Having the idea isn’t ongoing work.

checks.scenario: Yusuf in Jammu codes and builds apps, but dislikes talking to customers. He wants a co-founder for his campus bus-tracking app.
checks.question: Who would complement Yusuf best?
options: Another strong coder who could build features twice as fast
A classmate who has sold 50 event passes on campus this term
His closest friend, who is excited but has done neither job
A senior who wants the co-founder title for 3 hours a month
checks.hint: Think about what a co-founder adds to a team, beyond more of the same.
checks.why: Complementary skills mean one builds and the other sells. The classmate has already shown they can sell on campus. A second coder adds what Yusuf already has. Excitement isn’t a skill, and 3 hours a month isn’t the same commitment.

checks.scenario: Ankit and his sister run a vegetable-box delivery service in Gwalior. They are writing down three team habits.
checks.question: Which line is a habit they can act on?
options: We always put our customers first, whatever happens
We note down big decisions whenever we find the time
We stay honest with each other about everything
We write each decision in our shared Google Doc that day
checks.hint: For each line, ask: at the end of a week, could they tell whether they kept it?
checks.why: It is a specific action with a deadline, so each week they can see whether they kept it. Putting customers first and staying honest are values, not actions. “Whenever we find the time” never tells them they have slipped.

quiz.title: Leaving after 30 months
quiz.scenario: Three founders in Ahmedabad agreed in writing that Kiran owns 40% of their company, vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. Kiran leaves after 30 months.
quiz.question: How much of the company has Kiran earned?
options: 40%, because her full share was agreed in writing
10%, because only the part at the one-year cliff has vested
25%, because 30 of the 48 months of her 40% have vested
0%, because she left before the four years were over
quiz.explanation: At the one-year cliff a quarter vests, and the rest vests month by month. At 30 months she has earned 30 ÷ 48 = 62.5% of her 40%, which is 25% of the company. The unearned 15% stays with the business.
quiz.why_wrong: 40% ignores vesting: the agreement says she earns her shares over time. 10% counts only the quarter that vests at the cliff and forgets the 18 months after it. 0% mixes up the four-year vesting period with the one-year cliff, which she passed long ago.
quiz.learning_outcome: Work out vested equity: months served ÷ 48 × the share, once past the cliff.

quiz.title: Who decides
quiz.scenario: Asif and Leena run a phone-accessories business in Kozhikode and own it 50:50. Every week they argue about decisions, from Instagram posts to buying ₹15,000 of stock. Nothing about roles is written down.
quiz.question: Which written rule would best end the weekly arguments?
options: Leena owns marketing, Asif owns stock and money, and they decide jointly above ₹10,000
They both work on everything, and they discuss each decision until both of them agree
Asif makes every decision, because he was the one who had the idea for the business
They take turns, with one of them making all of the decisions in alternate weeks
quiz.explanation: Most founder arguments are about who decides. Giving each area one owner, who listens and then decides, ends the small arguments, and a rule for big spending keeps both of them involved where it matters most.
quiz.why_wrong: “Both on everything” is the setup that causes the weekly arguments. Who had the idea says nothing about who should decide each area, and it leaves Leena with no say. Alternating weeks makes decisions depend on the calendar, and each can undo the other’s choices.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give each area of the business one owner, and agree how joint decisions are made.

quiz.title: Briefing a designer
quiz.scenario: Priyanka needs a logo for her tuition centre in Ranchi. She has ₹5,000 and wants it within two weeks.
quiz.question: Which brief is best to send a freelance designer?
options: “A cool, modern logo for my tuition centre, quite soon. I will pay well and I trust your creative ideas.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 paid in full once our centre starts making a profit.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 by UPI, half now and half on delivery, with source files.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 paid in full today. Please send the final logo as a JPG.”
quiz.explanation: It gives the deliverable, the deadline, the budget and the payment plan, and asks for the original files so Priyanka can change the logo later. Half now and half on delivery is fair to both sides.
quiz.why_wrong: “Cool and modern” and “will pay well” give the designer nothing definite to work to or agree on. Paying only when the centre makes a profit pushes her business risk onto the designer. Paying everything today removes any check on delivery, and a JPG alone means she can’t edit the logo later.
quiz.learning_outcome: Brief a freelancer with deliverables, deadline, budget, payment terms and files.

quiz.title: Before saying yes
quiz.scenario: Gaurav, a commerce student in Kanpur, wants to start a used-furniture resale business. His classmate Saloni, who has sold things online before, wants to join him as a co-founder. They have never worked together.
quiz.question: What should they do before agreeing to be co-founders?
options: Run a two-week test together, and agree on hours, job offers and disagreements
Sign a 50:50 split straight away, so that both of them feel fully committed
Compare their marks and CVs, to decide which of them should be the main founder
Wait to talk about roles and equity until the business is earning some money
quiz.explanation: Working together on a small project, such as an MVP test, shows how they actually work as a team. Agreeing on weekly hours, what happens if one takes a job offer, and how to settle disagreements prevents the most common co-founder break-ups.
quiz.why_wrong: Signing 50:50 first locks in a deal before they know whether they work well together. Marks and CVs say little about commitment or how someone handles disagreement. Waiting until there is money makes the talk harder, because there is more to argue over.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test a co-founder partnership and talk through commitment before committing.

questions.title: Ten different answers
questions.scenario: Riya plans a study-planner service for “all college students in Delhi”. She has done 10 interviews. Each person described a different problem: exam stress, hostel noise, too many apps, slow Wi-Fi and more.
questions.question: What does this tell her to do next?
options: Choose a smaller customer group, and interview people from that group
Build features that solve all ten problems, so that everyone is covered
Ask an AI chatbot which of the ten problems is the most common one
Interview 50 more Delhi students, so that a pattern becomes clear
questions.explanation: When people in a group describe the problem in completely different ways, the group is too broad. A smaller, specific group, such as first-year hostel students before semester exams, is likely to share one problem she can test.
questions.why_wrong: Ten features for ten problems is building before she knows which problem is real. A chatbot can’t tell her what real students experience; only real people from a sharper group can. More interviews from the same broad group will keep giving scattered answers.
questions.learning_outcome: Narrow the customer group when answers scatter.

questions.title: A big crore figure
questions.scenario: Faisal is planning a doubt-solving service for Class 12 students in Lucknow. A free AI chatbot told him the coaching market in India is worth thousands of crores, but gave no source he could open. His mentor asks him for a market estimate.
questions.question: What should he give his mentor?
options: The chatbot’s figure, with a clear note that it came from an AI tool
The chatbot’s figure, as long as a second chatbot gives a similar one
A bottom-up estimate from numbers he can check, with guesses marked
No estimate, since market size can’t be known before he launches
questions.explanation: An AI figure is usable only if he can open its source and check it. Counting the students he can reach, then multiplying by a marked guess of the share who would pay and by the price, gives an estimate he can defend and test.
questions.why_wrong: Saying a number came from AI doesn’t make it true. Two chatbots can repeat the same invented or out-of-date figure. A bottom-up estimate is possible before launch: it simply marks which numbers are guesses still to test.
questions.learning_outcome: Use only AI figures you can source; build estimates bottom-up.

questions.title: The problem is real
questions.scenario: Kavya interviewed 8 working parents in Kochi about weekday dinners. Seven already pay a neighbour or a tiffin service ₹3,000 to ₹4,000 a month. She plans a weekly dinner subscription at ₹3,500 a month, paid in advance. Nobody has paid her anything yet.
questions.question: What is her best next step?
options: Offer a one-week trial on WhatsApp, and ask for payment in advance by UPI
Build a subscription app, since the interviews show the problem is real
Interview 20 more parents about how they manage weekday dinners now
Spend ₹5,000 on Instagram ads to see how many parents click on her page
questions.explanation: Her interviews already show the problem is real: parents spend money on it now. What she doesn’t know is whether they will pay her in advance, her riskiest assumption. A WhatsApp trial with a UPI advance tests exactly that, with free tools.
questions.why_wrong: An app takes weeks and still doesn’t test whether parents will pay her. More interviews about past behaviour repeat what she already knows. Ad clicks measure curiosity, not payment, and spend money before anyone has paid.
questions.learning_outcome: Move from evidence of a problem to an MVP that tests payment.

questions.title: Fourteen yeses
questions.scenario: Before his test, Aman wrote: “At least 5 of 20 hostel students pay a ₹100 advance for laundry pickup within 3 days.” After 3 days, 14 students said they would definitely use it, and 3 paid the advance.
questions.question: How should Aman report the result to his mentor?
options: A success: 14 of 20 (70%) want the service, far above his goal of 5
Goal missed: 3 paid, not 5, so he should ask why the others didn’t pay
Goal met, if he moves it to 3 of 20, since his first goal was too strict
A failure: only 3 of 20 paid, so he should drop the laundry idea now
questions.explanation: His goal was about paying, and he wrote it before the test: 3 is fewer than 5. The 14 “definitely” answers are promises, the bottom rung. Three real payments still matter, so asking the students who said yes but didn’t pay what stopped them shows what to change before he tests again.
questions.why_wrong: Counting promises as the result swaps the measure after the test. Moving the goal to 3 makes any result a success, which is exactly what writing it first prevents. Dropping the idea ignores three real payments and a gap he can investigate.
questions.learning_outcome: Report a test honestly against its goal; promises are not payments.

questions.title: The maybe
questions.scenario: Two days ago, a customer told Zoya “maybe next week” about her ₹999 skincare kit. Zoya sent one follow-up message yesterday. There is no reply yet.
questions.question: What should Zoya do now?
options: Message her every day until she gives a clear yes or no
Add her to a broadcast list to see every new product
Send one short message with a clear next step, then stop
Ask a mutual friend to remind her that she said maybe
questions.explanation: One or two short follow-ups are polite and useful; after that, silence is an answer. A clear next step, such as “Shall I keep one for you for Saturday?”, makes it easy to reply.
questions.why_wrong: Daily messages feel like pressure and can lose her as a future customer. A broadcast list sends her messages she didn’t ask for. Asking a friend to remind her adds social pressure, which can harm trust and the friendship.
questions.learning_outcome: Follow up once or twice with a clear next step, then stop.

questions.title: The screenshot
questions.scenario: A buyer sends Mohit a screenshot of a ₹600 UPI payment for two T-shirts. Mohit labels his WhatsApp Business chats “New”, “Paid” and “Delivered”.
questions.question: When should he label this chat “Paid”?
options: As soon as the screenshot arrives, since it shows the payment
When the ₹600 shows as received in his own bank or UPI app
When the buyer sends a message confirming that they have paid
After delivery, when the buyer says the T-shirts have arrived
questions.explanation: A screenshot can be faked, or can show a payment that later failed. The only proof is the money in his own account, so he checks his bank or UPI app before he labels the chat and sends the order.
questions.why_wrong: A screenshot is easy to fake or edit. A message saying “I’ve paid” is not money received. Waiting until delivery mixes two steps: he should confirm the payment before he sends the order, not after.
questions.learning_outcome: Count a sale as paid only when the money reaches your account.

questions.title: Two channels, one margin
questions.scenario: Tanvi sells homemade granola in Mumbai. Each order brings her ₹60 of contribution, and a customer orders about twice. In her ₹1,000 test, ₹600 of samples at a yoga studio won 6 customers, and a ₹400 boosted post won 2 customers.
questions.question: What should she do with her next marketing budget?
options: Put it into the boosted post, since a post reaches many more people
Split it between both channels again, since each one won customers
Stop spending, since one ₹60 order earns back neither ₹100 nor ₹200
Put it into the studio, where a customer costs ₹100 and brings ₹120
questions.explanation: Studio CAC is ₹600 ÷ 6 = ₹100 and post CAC is ₹400 ÷ 2 = ₹200. A customer brings about 2 × ₹60 = ₹120, so studio customers earn back their cost and post customers lose ₹80 each. One small test is a hint, so she should keep measuring.
questions.why_wrong: Reach doesn’t help if the post’s customers cost ₹200 and bring ₹120. Splitting again ignores what the test showed. Comparing one ₹60 order with the CAC forgets that customers order about twice.
questions.learning_outcome: Compare each channel’s CAC with what a customer brings.

questions.title: For everyone who loves food
questions.scenario: Kiran in Chennai sells ready-to-cook dosa batter. Her positioning is “for everyone who loves good food”, and she posts a little on four platforms. After a month she has 2 orders. Her interviews showed that couples who both work need quick breakfasts, and hear about home sellers through apartment WhatsApp groups.
questions.question: What is the best advice for her?
options: Add two more platforms, so that her posts reach more people each week
Boost every post she has made, so that more people see each of them
Offer 50% off for a month, so that more people are tempted to try it
Aim at working couples, through their apartments’ WhatsApp groups
questions.explanation: Her interviews already name the customer and the problem, and show where those customers look for sellers. Narrow positioning and one channel they use, with each group admin’s permission, give her effort a chance to show a result.
questions.why_wrong: More platforms spread the same thin effort further. Boosting posts with no clear customer pays to reach people who may not want batter. A big discount attracts bargain-hunters and hides whether her real customers value the product.
questions.learning_outcome: Use interview evidence to set positioning and pick one channel.

questions.title: Ten lakh from investors
questions.scenario: Rahul, a second-year student in Hyderabad, has an idea for a campus delivery app. He has no customers yet. He plans to message 100 angel investors on LinkedIn, asking for ₹10 lakh.
questions.question: What is the best advice for Rahul?
options: Send all 100 messages, since just one investor saying yes would be enough
Win first paying users with a small MVP, and ask the E-cell for advice
Ask his family for the ₹10 lakh instead, with nothing written down
Take a ₹10 lakh bank loan, so that he gives away none of his shares
questions.explanation: Investors are rare at the idea stage, and they look for evidence such as paying customers. A small MVP gets that evidence cheaply, and his E-cell or incubator can advise him and later make warm, double opt-in introductions.
questions.why_wrong: A hundred identical messages to strangers are spam, and with no customers there is little for an investor to back. Family money with nothing written down risks the relationship: write whether it is a gift, a loan or a share. A big loan for an untested idea leaves him owing money whether or not it works.
questions.learning_outcome: Get evidence before chasing investors, and use your network well.

questions.title: The canteen deal
questions.scenario: Divya’s college canteen in Jaipur has agreed to stock her millet energy bars and keep a share of each sale. They shook hands on it yesterday.
questions.question: What should Divya do next?
options: Rely on the handshake, since a written note could look like mistrust
Write one paragraph on who does what, who earns what and how to end it
Get a long contract from an AI chatbot and ask the canteen to sign it
Write down the share of each sale that the canteen keeps, and nothing else
questions.explanation: A short written note covers what partners usually fall out over: who does what (stocking, display, restocking), who earns what, and how either side can end the deal. It protects the relationship as well as the money.
questions.why_wrong: A handshake leaves each side remembering different terms. A long AI-written contract that neither side has read may contain terms nobody intended, and can put a small partner off. Writing only the share leaves out who restocks, what happens to unsold bars and how to end the deal.
questions.learning_outcome: Write partnership terms down in one short paragraph.

questions.title: Phone stands
questions.scenario: Ravi sells personalised phone stands for ₹400 through a payment link. Each stand costs ₹220 in materials, packing and delivery. Today he checked the gateway’s own pricing page, which lists a total fee of 2.36% of each payment. His CAC is ₹150, and each customer buys one stand.
questions.question: How much does each customer leave him after the CAC?
questions.explanation: The fee is 2.36% of ₹400 = ₹9.44, so contribution is ₹400 − ₹220 − ₹9.44 = ₹170.56. Taking away the ₹150 CAC leaves ₹20.56 from each customer.
questions.why_wrong: ₹30.00 leaves out the payment fee, which comes out of every sale. ₹170.56 is the contribution per stand, before the cost of winning the customer. ₹25.75 works out the fee on the ₹180 margin instead of on the full ₹400 payment.
questions.learning_outcome: Include a dated payment fee in contribution, then compare with CAC.

questions.title: Leaving before the cliff
questions.scenario: Neel, Farah and Joseph signed a split of 30%, 35% and 35%, each vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. Neel leaves after 11 months to take a job.
questions.question: How much of the company does Neel keep?
options: 0%: his 30% stays with the business, for those who do the work
7.5%: a quarter of his 30%, and the rest stays with the business
About 6.9%: 11 of 48 months, and the rest stays with the business
30%: shares that were signed for can’t be taken back from a founder
questions.explanation: With a one-year cliff, nothing vests until the first year is complete. Neel left at 11 months, so he keeps none, and his unvested shares stay with the business for the founders who stay and do the work.
questions.why_wrong: 7.5% treats him as if he had reached the cliff, but he left a month before it. 6.9% counts month by month from the start, ignoring the cliff. 30% ignores the vesting they signed: the agreement itself says shares are earned over time.
questions.learning_outcome: Apply the cliff: leaving before it means no shares vest.

questions.title: A six-week intern
questions.scenario: Your E-cell offers you a first-year student as an intern for six weeks, to help with your snack-box business’s Instagram page.
questions.question: Which plan is fairest and most useful?
options: “Help with marketing and anything else that comes up. Flexible hours; let’s see how it goes.”
“Plan and post 3 Reels a week, 8 hours a week. You learn content testing; I review weekly. Pay agreed now.”
“Plan and post 3 Reels a week, full-time, to show commitment. Pay will be a small share of the company later.”
“Run the whole Instagram page on your own for six weeks. You get a certificate at the end if the page grows.”
questions.explanation: It names the work, the hours, what the intern will learn, who guides them, and pay agreed before they start. The intern learns something real, and the business gets a clear piece of work done.
questions.why_wrong: “Help with marketing and anything else” is the vague internship where the intern learns little and little gets done. Full-time hours for an unclear future share asks a lot and promises nothing definite. Running the page alone, for a certificate only if it grows, gives no guidance and no fair pay.
questions.learning_outcome: Brief an intern with the work, hours, learning, guidance and pay.

questions.title: The one-page plan
questions.scenario: A mentor reviews Sana’s plan for a weekly snack box in Pune. She has 7 interviews, 3 introductions and 2 paid advances. Her price is ₹199, and each box costs ₹170 to make and deliver. Her ₹1,000 test on her one channel, college WhatsApp groups, won 8 customers. Most customers buy only once. She plans to spend ₹10,000 on marketing next month.
questions.question: What is the most serious problem in her plan?
options: Seven interviews are too few to show that the problem is real for her customers
She markets on only one channel, so she misses the customers on other platforms
Each customer brings ₹29 but costs ₹125 to win, so more marketing deepens the loss
Her plan names no investor, so she has no way to pay for ₹10,000 of marketing
questions.explanation: Contribution is ₹199 − ₹170 = ₹29 a box, and CAC is ₹1,000 ÷ 8 = ₹125. With one purchase each, every new customer loses her about ₹96, so ₹10,000 more marketing would lose money faster. She needs a higher price, lower costs or repeat orders before she spends more.
questions.why_wrong: Seven interviews with introductions and paid advances already reach the top rungs of the ladder, which is enough at this stage. Starting with one channel is right, not a weakness. Investor money would only pay for the losses; the unit economics must work first.
questions.learning_outcome: Read a whole plan and find the problem that matters most: losing money on every customer.

questions.title: AI and interview notes
questions.scenario: Rohan has notes from 6 customer interviews, including names and phone numbers. He wants a free AI chatbot to group the notes into patterns for his mentor.
questions.question: Which way of using the chatbot is sound?
options: Paste in the full notes so the chatbot has every detail, and send its summary on
Remove names and numbers, ask for themes, and check each theme against his notes
Remove names and numbers, and ask it to add 20 realistic interviews for a bigger sample
Remove names and numbers, ask for themes, and send them on as they are, since it read all six
questions.explanation: Removing personal details protects the people who spoke to him. Grouping notes is a good job for AI, but chatbots can overstate or invent a pattern, so each theme must be checked against what people actually said before it goes to his mentor.
questions.why_wrong: Pasting names and phone numbers shares people’s personal details without need. AI-made interviews are synthetic users, not evidence, and they would hide the real pattern. Sending the themes unchecked trusts the AI, when it can report a pattern that nobody mentioned.
questions.learning_outcome: Protect interviewees’ details and check every AI summary against the source.

project.brief: Over about two weeks, with your mentor’s guidance, take one real business idea (your own, or one from your campus) from a guess to evidence. Talk to at least 5 real people from your customer group, and win at least one commitment: a next meeting, an introduction, a trial booked or a payment. Then write a one-page plan that a mentor or an early supporter could act on. Your mentor helps you choose the idea and the customer group, and reviews your interview script before you start. Plan for about 8 hours of work spread over the two weeks: conversations take time to arrange, so start them in the first week.
deliverables: A problem statement for one named customer group, with a bottom-up market estimate whose numbers each have a source you checked

An interview log of at least 5 real conversations (names removed, with permission), each with the date, the person’s role and what they had already done about the problem, plus a summary of the patterns

Proof of at least one commitment (such as a UPI payment screenshot with personal details hidden, a booked trial, or an introduction), with a note on which rung of the evidence ladder each piece of evidence reaches
Your MVP and the result of testing it with 5 users, set against the success goal you wrote before the test

A one-page plan: the customer, the offer and price, unit economics and a one-month cash flow in rupees, the first marketing channel, who owns which area (if you have co-founders, the equity split and vesting you have agreed in writing; a solo founder writes the split and vesting they would offer a co-founder), and the next 30 days
A note to your mentor on what the evidence changed in your idea, and where you used AI and how you checked it

rubric.name: Evidence quality
rubric.description: At least 5 real conversations about past behaviour, each placed on the right rung of the evidence ladder, and at least one real commitment shown

rubric.name: Problem and customer
rubric.description: One named customer group and its problem in their own words, with a bottom-up estimate whose sources are checked and guesses marked

rubric.name: MVP test
rubric.description: The riskiest assumption is named, the success goal was written before the test, and the result is reported honestly against it

rubric.name: Price and money
rubric.description: A price set between cost and the next best option, with contribution, CAC, dated fees and a one-month cash flow that add up

rubric.name: Plan and judgement
rubric.description: The next 30 days and the channel follow from the evidence, each area has one owner, the equity split and vesting are written (agreed, or proposed if solo), and every use of AI is named and checked
